newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Bonanza for OPEC as oil rivals falter.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bonanza for OPEC as oil rivals falter.

text.p: OPEC will benefit from higher than expected demand for its oil for the rest of this year and well into 1997 as supplies from rival sources fail to match earlier forecasts, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Friday.
The world's oil supply-demand position must now also take into account the crisis in Iraq which will put on hold that country's return to the market.

The Paris-based agency, which serves as the West's energy watchdog, revised down its projections for supply from producers outside the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries for the last six months of 1996 by 300,000 barrels per day (bpd).
"Primarily as a result of decreases in projections of non-OPEC supplies, the call (demand) on OPEC crude...has been increased," the IEA said in its latest Oil Market Report.
The IEA raised its forecasts for demand for OPEC oil by 300,000 bpd to 24.2 million bpd in the third quarter and by 400,000 bpd to 25.6 million in the fourth quarter.
"This is mildly bullish for OPEC. The IEA was the last source still holding out for a big rise in non-OPEC supply in the fourth quarter," said Mehdi Varzi, oil analyst at Kleinwort Benson.
"The rise is still going to be there but it's not as big as people thought."

A combination of weather-related disruptions, terrorist attacks in Latin America and technical problems at North Sea fields led the IEA to reduce its forecast for non-OPEC supply, which is still running well above year-ago levels.

"It looks broadly constructive for the market due to the lower forcasts for non-OPEC production in Asia and Latin America which leaves a bit more room for OPEC," said Chris Buckley, oil analyst at Morgan Stanley.

World oil output in August averaged 71.9 million bpd, down from July's 72.1 million bpd. Non-OPEC production dipped to 43.4 million bpd in August, while OPEC pumped an average of 25.81 million, 70,000 bpd fewer than in July.

With the IEA increasing its forecast for OPEC demand in the first quarter of 1997 by 300,000 bpd and the recent Iraqi crisis putting on hold Baghdad's return to the market under a U.N. oil-for-food scheme, the cartel's members may see windfall revenues continue despite producing consistently above seld-imposed quotas.

"There is clearly higher demand and lower than expected non-OPEC output combined with the loss of Iraqi oil...I would have thought the scene is set for further price strength," said Stephen O'Sullivan, associate director of MC Securities Ltd.

Oil prices currently stand about $5 a barrel above levels seen this time last year, boosted by a combination of a cold 1995/96 northern winter, robust world economic growth, key supply disruptions and rising Middle East tension.

Analysts said it was highly unlikely that such a bullish cocktail would be repeated next year but warned that against a background of low stocks and the approach of winter, prices could move higher again before returning to more normal levels.
"The upside is limited but now we're hostage to two things - winter weather and the possibility of tension increasing again over Iraq," said Varzi.

Oil stocks held by industry in the Organisation of Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries fell by 200,000 bpd in July -- the first time stocks fell in July for 11 years -- to stand 153 million barrels below the peak in 1995, the IEA said.
